To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the gel network structure of two-component gelled systems based on a lysine-based dendron (Dendr-1,2) and a rigid aromatic diamine is controlled by the stoichiometry and the component selection processes.

The gel network formed from a combination of a lysine-based dendron (Lys-D) and an aromatic diamine (1,4-DB) always consists of a 1 : 1 mixture of components, irrespective of the molyar ratio of the components.

two-component gel systems, based on a L-lysinederived dendron and a diamine spacer, can be used to control the formation of ternary complexes with a third component, and that the gel network is able to select the diamine component from mixtures of similar aromatic diamines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and synthesis of functional materials based on supramolecular chemistry.
the design and investigation of two-component systems capable of forming supramolecular networks.
the self-assembly of supramolecular materials, and in particular the development of new soft materials with novel properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gel network formed by a 1: 1 mixture of dendrons and diamine, with the dendrons preferentially recognising the aromatic component (1,4-DB).
the dendron/diamines are able to self-assemble into a 1: 1 complex in a component-selecting manner.
the dendron/diamines system investigated here is capable of forming gels in a component-selectable and stoichiometric manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two component gels can tolerate excess of one component in the liquid phase, and the gel network is able to select the component that it is most compatible with in the solid phase.

we can tune the self-assembly process in a two-component system by changing the molar ratio between two gelators, and we can also control the selectivity of the gel network by changing the nature of the aromatic diamine component.
we have shown how two-component gel systems, based on a combination between a lysine-based dendron (1) and a diamine spacer (2), can be used to control hierarchical assembly in three-component gels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two-component gel systems are capable of self-selecting their components and forming a 1:2 complex, which is a unique feature of this class of materials.
the gel network can tolerate a significant excess (up to 50%) of diamine in a liquid phase, but that the network can still be formed from mixtures of diamines in excess.
the gel network is capable of selectively assembling from mixtures of diamines and is able to tolerate a large excess of diamine before disruption.
